# 2. Technical details


```{r}
# Import original data
listings <- read.csv("https://ajohns24.github.io/data/NYC_airbnb_kaggle.csv")
nbhd     <- read.csv("https://ajohns24.github.io/data/NYC_nbhd_kaggle.csv")

# Wrangle this into the final airbnb data
set.seed(253)
airbnb <- listings %>% 
  filter(price > 0, price < 1000) %>% 
  sample_n(size = 5000) %>% 
  rename(neighbourhood = neighbourhood_cleansed) %>% 
  left_join(nbhd) %>% 
  select(-neighbourhood, -amenities, -host_response_rate, -calendar_updated)

# Data wrangling and removign columns
airbnb_model <- airbnb %>% 
  select(-id, -square_feet)
```

The main obstcale we came across while working with this dataset was the missing data. One of the coulmns which is square_feet was missing more that 4900 out of 5000 rows, hence why we removed it from the airbnb_model because it was not giving us any significant data. However, since square_feet wasn't the only column with missing data, to address the remaining missing values across other predictors without discarding valuable observations, we implemented $K$-nearest neighbors imputation with five neighbors within our preprocessing recipe. Continuous missing features were estimated using the mean values of a listing’s five most similar neighbors, whereas categorical variables were imputed using the neighbor mode. Imputation was performed within each cross-validation fold so that held-out listings never informed the imputed values.

**Model Specification and Tuning**

Because rental listings feature naturally correlated characteristics such as room count, bathroom count, and overall guest capacity, standard linear regression risks variance inflation due to multicollinearity. To overcome this limitation, we selected LASSO regression, an L1-regularized linear model. LASSO applies a penalty parameter that shrinks uninformative coefficient estimates toward zero, automatically zeroing out redundant features to deliver both predictive precision and parsimonious interpretability. We established a regularized grid search across 50 penalty values ranging from 0.001 to 10 on a logarithmic scale, evaluating model accuracy through 10-fold cross-validated Mean Absolute Error.

```{r}
# Define model specification
airbnb_lasso_spec <- linear_reg() |> 
  set_mode("regression") |> 
  set_engine("glmnet") |> 
  set_args(mixture = 1, penalty = tune())

# Define recipe preprocessing steps
airbnb_variable_recipe <- recipe(price ~ ., data = airbnb_model) |> 
  step_string2factor(all_nominal_predictors()) |> 
  step_impute_knn(all_predictors(), neighbors = 5) |> 
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) 

# Bundle into workflow
airbnb_lasso_workflow <- workflow() |> 
  add_recipe(airbnb_variable_recipe) |> 
  add_model(airbnb_lasso_spec)

# Tune model over cross-validation grid
set.seed(253)
airbnb_lasso_models <- airbnb_lasso_workflow |> 
  tune_grid(
    grid = grid_regular(penalty(range = c(-3, 1)), levels = 50),
    resamples = vfold_cv(airbnb_model, v = 10),
    metrics = metric_set(mae)
  )
```

**Tuning Evaluation and Penalty Selection**

We evaluated 50 regularized penalty values ($\lambda$ between $[0.001, 10]$) on a logarithmic scale across 10-fold cross-validation using Mean Absolute Error (MAE) as our evaluation metric.

```{r}
# Select optimal penalty parameter
best_penalty <- airbnb_lasso_models %>% 
  select_best(metric = "mae") 
    
collect_metrics(airbnb_lasso_models) |> 
  filter(penalty == best_penalty$penalty)

# Plot cross-validation results
autoplot(airbnb_lasso_models) + 
  scale_x_continuous() + 
  xlab(expression(lambda)) +
  labs(
    title = "CV MAE vs Tuning parameter",
    caption = "Figure 3"
  )

parsimonious_penalty <- airbnb_lasso_models |> 
  select_by_one_std_err(metric = "mae", desc(penalty))

collect_metrics(airbnb_lasso_models) |> 
  filter(penalty == parsimonious_penalty$penalty)
```

The penalty value that minimised cross-validated error achieved a Mean Absolute Error of $46.48 while retaining 18 predictor variables. However, to prevent overfitting and produce a cleaner explanation of price drivers, we adopted the one-standard-error rule to select a more parsimonious model. This simpler specification selected 12 non-zero predictors with a cross-validated Mean Absolute Error of $47.10. Accepting an error increase of merely 62 cents per night allowed us to remove six unnecessary variables, achieving an optimal balance between predictive accuracy and statistical simplicity.

```{r}
# Finalize workflow and fit full model using best penalty
airbnb_final_1_lasso <- airbnb_lasso_workflow |> 
  finalize_workflow(parameters = best_penalty) |> 
  fit(data = airbnb_model)

airbnb_final_1_lasso %>%
  tidy() %>%
  filter(estimate != 0) %>% 
  arrange(desc(abs(estimate)))

# Finalize workflow and fit full model using parsimonious penalty
airbnb_final_lasso <- airbnb_lasso_workflow |> 
  finalize_workflow(parameters = parsimonious_penalty) |> 
  fit(data = airbnb_model)

# View non-zero coefficient estimates
airbnb_final_lasso %>%
  tidy() %>%
  filter(estimate != 0) %>% 
  arrange(desc(abs(estimate)))
```

On unseen listing data, our finalised parsimonious model predicts nightly rates with an expected average error of approximately $47.10. An examination of the non-zero model coefficients demonstrates that room category serves as the single strongest driver of rental pricing. Relative to renting an entire home or apartment, listing a private room reduces the expected nightly price by approximately $54, while offering a shared room lowers the predicted price by $57, while holding all other listing features constant.

Geographic location demonstrates the second largest impact on rental valuation. Controlling for physical size and amenities, listings situated in Manhattan command a premium of roughly $40 per night compared to baseline listings located in the Bronx. Finally, physical property capacity scales predictably: each additional bathroom increases expected nightly price by about $30, each additional bedroom adds approximately $22, and each additional guest accommodated raises the price by $16.
